Field observations of Buff-rumped warbler (Myiothlypis fulvicauda) nests in lowland Peruvian forests reveal that newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet body mass of just 4.2 grams [Ww0 = 4.2 grams]. This altricial nestling mass is consistent with the values reported for other parulid warblers and reflects the substantial energetic investment required for the rapid growth phase that follows hatching at an incubation temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] and an incubation duration of 17 days [ab = 17 days]. The relatively brief incubation period compared to larger tropical passerines may be an adaptation to reduce exposure to nest predation, which is intense in Neotropical understory habitats. Once hatched, the nestlings depend entirely on biparental provisioning, and their early development proceeds quickly, with feather tracts becoming visible within the first week and eyes opening by the ninth day post-hatching.

Under the typical thermal conditions of active metabolism in this species, which cluster around a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs at 13.5 days after hatching [tx = 13.5 days after hatching]. This represents a relatively short nestling phase for a warbler of its size, suggesting that the selective pressure to leave the vulnerable nest environment is strong. The timing of fledging is closely tied to the development of flight feathers and the achievement of sufficient neuromuscular coordination for short flights to nearby cover. Parental provisioning continues for several weeks after nest departure, during which time the fledglings refine their foraging skills while still receiving supplemental food from the adults. The dense undergrowth of their riparian habitat provides ample concealment for these inexperienced young birds as they transition to independence.

Sexual maturation in Buff-rumped warbler is attained at 40.5 days after hatching [tp = 40.5 days after hatching], measured under the same thermoneutral body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early onset of reproductive capability is notable for a tropical passerine and may be linked to their high adult mortality rates, which select for early breeding to maximize lifetime reproductive success. The development of gonadal tissue and the onset of hormonal cycles associated with territorial behavior are accelerated compared to many temperate-zone migratory warblers, likely because the stable, resource-rich environment of Neotropical lowland forests allows year-round maintenance of a high metabolic rate. First-year birds often attempt to establish territories adjacent to adult pairs, though success in securing a breeding site depends heavily on the availability of suitable understory vegetation near streams.

The first successful brood is typically produced at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], again at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This one-year delay between sexual maturity and first reproduction suggests that young birds invest considerable time in territory acquisition, mate selection, and construction of the domed nest structures characteristic of the species. Females lay two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a modest reproductive output that is typical of tropical insectivores with extended parental care. The ultimate wet weight for adult females is 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams], representing a substantial increase from the natal mass and reflecting the accretion of reproductive tissues and fat reserves necessary to support egg formation.

The maximum recorded longevity for this species in natural populations is 7.8 years [am = 7.8 years], documented under field conditions approximating a core body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a small-bodied passerine and suggests a slow life-history pace compared to North American migratory warblers of similar mass. Basal metabolic rate, measured via flow-through respirometry in post-absorptive, resting individuals at thermoneutrality, averages 63.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 63.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This comparatively elevated metabolic expenditure is consistent with the high activity levels required for year-round territorial defense in a competitive tropical avifauna and is supported by a diet dominated by arthropods gleaned from leaf litter and bark surfaces in humid riparian corridors.
